title: Between a man and his heart
hook: Allah comes between a person and his heart (8:24)
carry: he is nearer than my heart

segments.voice: Yesterday: rama, you did not throw. Your line was it wasn't only me. Who did you credit? Today, from the hand to the heart, and a verse that goes closer than anything. Day four hundred eighteen.

Pick up an old diary, and the person who wrote it can seem like a stranger: in love with things since dropped, afraid of things that never came, sure of plans that now look foolish. Hearts change. In Arabic the heart is qalb, and the same root gives the word for turning: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ called God muqallib al-qulub, the Turner of hearts. The heart is the thing that turns. Surah eight has a verse about who stands at that turning point.
screen: `AN OLD DIARY, A STRANGER.` → `QALB — THE THING THAT TURNS.` → `WHO STANDS AT THE TURNING?`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-four opens with an invitation: O you who believe, respond to Allah and the messenger when he calls you to what gives you life. Then, in Pickthall's words: “know that Allah cometh in between the man and his own heart,” and that to Him you will be gathered. What does it mean for Allah to come between a person and their heart? Early commentators gave two readings, and both are still taught. One: Allah is closer to a person than their own heart. Surah fifty says He is nearer to a person than the vein in their neck. In this reading, the heart is the most inward thing a person has, and He is nearer still. Two: Allah can turn a heart. He can stand between a person and what their heart wants, or between a person and the faith they assumed they'd always have. So, the verse implies, respond to the call while your heart is open. Don't assume you'll feel the same next year. That second reading sits behind a du'a the Prophet is reported to have said often. In Tirmidhi's collection, his wife Umm Salamah says it was the du'a he made most: ya muqallib al-qulub, thabbit qalbi 'ala dinik. O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm on Your religion. When asked why, he said every heart is held between two fingers of the Most Merciful, and He turns it as He wills. That's from a man whose heart his followers trusted completely, asking for steadiness, every day. The heart is not a fortress. It's a door on a hinge, and the verse says who holds the hinge.
screen: `RESPOND TO WHAT GIVES YOU LIFE.` · `NEARER THAN YOUR OWN HEART.` · `HE CAN TURN A HEART.` · `O TURNER OF HEARTS.` · then, large: `BETWEEN A MAN AND HIS HEART.`

segments.voice: Sit, and put a hand on your chest if that feels right. Feel the heartbeat, or just the warmth. Think of one way your heart has turned lately, toward something good or away from it. Notice it without judgment. If you pray, you can say the Prophet's du'a, slowly, in Arabic or English: O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm. If you don't, simply rest with the verse's picture of a heart that can turn. The bell holds the time.
Muqallib al-qulub, the Turner of hearts. Surah eight, verse twenty-four: Allah comes between a person and their heart, nearer than it, and able to turn it.
Your line: he is nearer than my heart. Today, when your mood flips, remember the hinge, and who holds it. Day four hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Muslims repeat the Prophet's du'a, ya muqallib al-qulub, thabbit qalbi 'ala dinik (O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm on Your religion), especially in hard or uncertain times.

fork.setup: Umm Salamah hears the Prophet ask, again and again, for a steady heart. what does he answer when she asks why?
options: he was worried about one companion.
every heart is between two fingers of the Most Merciful, who turns it as He wills.
fork.reveal: hearts turn, so he asked for steadiness every day: no heart, even his, was treated as a fortress.

original.note: Arabic: He comes between a person and his heart (8:24).

trapdoor: what you thought: God knows what's in your heart.
what it means: Allah is nearer than your heart and can turn it, so respond to what gives you life while your heart is open.
what a scholar hears: al-Tabari records both readings; the 'turning' reading is linked to Ibn Abbas, and the hadith of the two fingers (Muslim 2654) is read by some without asking how.
